Install Godot 4.7 and the export templat:
Godot ships as a single executable with no installer. Download the **standard** build, not .NET, unless you want C# — this curriculum is GDScript throughout.

Put it somewhere permanent and make it executable: `chmod +x Godot_v4.7-stable_linux.x86_64`.

Then, separately: **Editor > Manage Export Templates > Download and Install**. These are the engine binaries your game gets bundled with. They are ~1 GB, they are version-locked to the editor, and nothing will export without them. Doing it now means stage 10 is not a download.

Check `Help > About` and write the exact version down. A project opened in a newer editor is silently upgraded and cannot go back.
Make a project: renderer choice, folder:
**Project Manager > Create**. Three decisions:

· **Renderer** — Forward+, Mobile, or Compatibility. For 2D, choose **Compatibility**: it runs on the widest hardware, including old GPUs and the web, and gives up almost nothing you need in 2D. It is changeable later in Project Settings but not casually.
· **Version control metadata** — Git, which writes a sane `.gitignore`.
· An empty folder of its own.

The project root becomes `res://`. Everything you reference in code is a `res://` path.

Open `project.godot` in a text editor and read it. It is an INI file: the main scene, the input map, the physics and rendering settings, the autoloads. Every Project Settings change you make lands here, which is why it is worth reading once before you change 40 things and cannot remember which.
The interface: Scene, FileSystem, Inspec:
Four docks and the viewport. Learn what each is *for* before touching anything:

· **Scene** (top left) — the node tree of the scene you have open. This is the thing you are building.
· **FileSystem** (bottom left) — `res://` on disk. Drag from here into the Scene dock or the viewport to instance.
· **Inspector** (right) — every property of the selected node. This is the same data your script's `@export` variables appear in.
· **Node** (right, tabbed with Inspector) — two lists: **Signals** and **Groups**. Most beginners never find this tab. It is where stage 5 happens.

Bottom panel: Output, Debugger, Audio, Animation, Shader Editor. They slide up when used.

Top centre switches **2D / 3D / Script / AssetLib**. `Ctrl+F1` through `Ctrl+F4` switch them from the keyboard.
The 2D viewport: pan, zoom, select, snap:
· **Pan** — middle-mouse drag, or space-drag.
· **Zoom** — scroll wheel. `Ctrl+0` resets to 100%.
· **Select** — `Q`. **Move** — `W`. **Rotate** — `E`. **Scale** — `S`.
· **Frame selection** — `F`. **Frame all** — `Shift+F`.

Clicking selects the topmost node; `Alt+click` cycles down through what is under the cursor. This is how you select something buried in a stack of sprites.

Snapping lives in the toolbar magnet icon: **Use Grid Snap** (`Shift+G`), and **Configure Snap** to set the step. For pixel art set the grid step to 1 and leave snapping on — a sprite at x = 40.3 is a blurry sprite.

The red-and-blue crosshair at origin is (0,0) of the current scene. The pink rectangle is the game window as configured in Project Settings.
Run the project, run the current scene,:
· **F5** — run the project, which runs the *main scene* set in Project Settings > Application > Run.
· **F6** — run the scene you currently have open, whatever it is. This is the one you will use constantly.
· **F7** — pause.
· **F8** — stop.

The first `F5` asks you to pick a main scene. Pick one; change it later in Project Settings.

The habit worth forming now: build each piece as its own scene and test it with `F6` in isolation. A player scene that only runs inside the whole game is a player scene you cannot debug.
The Output, Debugger, and remote Scene t:
While the game runs, the editor is still live and this is the part nobody uses:

· **Output** — everything `print()` writes, plus engine warnings. Clear it between runs.
· **Debugger** — on an error it jumps here and gives you a **stack trace**. Click any frame to open that line. The **Errors** tab collects warnings you would otherwise miss scrolling past.
· The **Scene dock switches to Remote** while running. Click **Remote** and you get the *live* tree of the running game. Select a node and the Inspector shows its real current values, and you can change them and see the effect immediately.

That last one is the single most useful debugging tool in the engine. Use it before you reach for `print()`.
Editor settings worth changing on day on:
**Editor > Editor Settings**. Search is at the top; these are the ones that matter:

· `interface/editor/display_scale` — if the UI is tiny or huge.
· `text_editor/behavior/indent/type` — Godot style is **tabs**. Leave it.
· `text_editor/completion/add_type_hints` — **on**. Autocomplete then writes `-> void` and typed arguments for you.
· `debugger/auto_switch_to_remote_scene_tree` — on, so the previous lesson's trick is automatic.
· `text_editor/appearance/whitespace/draw_tabs` — on. GDScript is indentation-significant; seeing it is not optional.
· `run/window_placement/rect` — put the running game somewhere that is not on top of the editor.

And in **Project Settings** for every pixel-art project: `rendering/textures/canvas_textures/default_texture_filter` = **Nearest**. Linear filtering blurs pixel art and the default is linear.
The built-in docs: F1, and Ctrl-click on:
Godot's reference is in the editor and matches your exact version, which no web result does.

· **F1** — search help. Type a class name.
· **Ctrl+click** any class name or built-in method in the script editor — jumps straight to its documentation page.
· In the docs for a class, read **Properties**, **Methods**, **Signals**, and the **Inherits** chain at the top. The inheritance chain is the part to actually read: `Sprite2D` inherits `Node2D` inherits `CanvasItem` inherits `Node`, and most of what a Sprite2D can do is defined in those parents.

The reflex to build: when you wonder what a node can do, open its class page and read the method list top to bottom. It takes two minutes and replaces an hour of searching.
A node is an object in a tree; a scene i:
The whole engine is this one idea, so get it exactly:

· A **node** is an object with a name, a position in a tree, and a type that gives it behaviour. `Sprite2D` draws a texture. `Timer` counts down. `Area2D` detects overlap.
· A **scene** is a tree of nodes **saved to a file** (`.tscn`). That is the only difference between a scene and a branch of nodes — the file.
· A saved scene can be **instanced** inside another scene, where it behaves as a single node.

So "scene" does not mean "level". A scene is a bullet, a button, a character, a whole level, or the entire game. Godot makes no distinction and neither should you.

The consequence that takes a while to sink in: **there is no prefab system, no entity system and no component system.** There is a tree of nodes, and files that hold trees of nodes.
Your first scene: Node2D root, Sprite2D:
Scene dock > **Other Node** (or `Ctrl+A`) > search `Node2D` > Create. Rename it `Player` — double-click, or `F2`.

With `Player` selected, `Ctrl+A` again > `Sprite2D`. It is created as a **child** of the selection. The Scene dock indentation is the tree.

Drag any PNG from the FileSystem dock onto the Sprite2D's **Texture** property in the Inspector. Or drag the PNG straight into the viewport and Godot offers to make the Sprite2D for you.

Why a `Node2D` root rather than the `Sprite2D` alone: the root is the thing you move, and everything else hangs off it. A character with a sprite, a collision shape and a health bar needs a parent to hold them together. Choosing the root type is a real decision — stage 4 covers which to pick.
Saving a scene as .tscn, and what the fi:
`Ctrl+S`. Godot asks for a path; put scenes in a folder structure that mirrors the game — `res://player/player.tscn`, not everything in the root.

Now open the `.tscn` in a text editor. It is plain text, and reading it once explains more than any tutorial:

```
[gd_scene load_steps=2 format=3 uid="uid://bxyz"]

[ext_resource type="Texture2D" uid="uid://c123" path="res://art/player.png" id="1_abc"]

[node name="Player" type="Node2D"]

[node name="Sprite2D" type="Sprite2D" parent="."]
texture = ExtResource("1_abc")
```

Three things to take from it: the file **references** external resources rather than embedding them; `parent="."` is how the tree is encoded; and **only non-default properties are written**. That last point is why `.tscn` files diff cleanly in git, and why a scene file is readable.
Instancing a scene inside another scene:
Make a second scene (`Node2D` root, call it `World`, save it). Then either:

· Scene dock > the **chain-link icon** > pick `player.tscn`, or
· drag `player.tscn` from FileSystem into the viewport.

You now have a `Player` node inside `World` with a small **film-clapper icon** beside it. Its children are hidden, because from `World`'s point of view it is one node.

In code the same thing is two lines:

```gdscript
const PlayerScene := preload("res://player/player.tscn")

var p := PlayerScene.instantiate()
add_child(p)
```

`instantiate()` builds the tree in memory; `add_child()` puts it in the live tree and *that* is when `_ready()` fires. Forgetting `add_child` is the most common beginner bug: the node exists, runs nothing, and draws nothing.
Editable children, and overriding an ins:
Select an instanced scene and change a property in the Inspector — the position, say. A **revert arrow** appears beside it. The override is stored in the *parent* scene, and the original `.tscn` is untouched. Changing the original still updates every instance for every property you have not overridden.

To reach *inside* an instance: right-click it > **Editable Children**. Its children appear and become editable, and those changes are stored as overrides too.

Use it sparingly. Every editable-children override is a divergence between the instance and its source, it is invisible unless you look, and it is a classic source of "why does this one enemy behave differently". If you need a real variant, make a *new scene* that inherits — next lesson.
Scene inheritance:
**Scene > New Inherited Scene** > pick a `.tscn`.

You get a scene whose entire tree is the parent's, greyed out, where you can override properties, add nodes, and attach a different script. Changes to the parent flow down.

This is how you make `enemy_archer.tscn` and `enemy_knight.tscn` from `enemy.tscn` without duplicating the tree.

The limits, which matter: you cannot delete an inherited node, you cannot reorder inherited nodes, and renaming a node in the parent breaks the child. Inheritance is good for "the same thing with different numbers and one extra node". For anything structurally different, make a separate scene and share the *script* instead — composition beats inheritance here as everywhere.
The node lifecycle: _init, _enter_tree,:
Learn the exact order, because the whole class of "null on startup" bugs is this:

1. `_init()` — the object exists. **No children, no tree, no `$` paths.** Nothing is safe here but setting plain variables.
2. `_enter_tree()` — the node is in the tree. Fires **parent first, then children**.
3. `_ready()` — fires **children first, then the parent**, depth-first. By the time your `_ready()` runs, every child's `_ready()` has already run.

That ordering is the useful part: in `_ready()` you can touch your children because they are initialised; you **cannot** assume your parent is.

Then every frame: `_process(delta)` as fast as the machine renders, and `_physics_process(delta)` at a fixed rate (60 Hz by default).

On the way out: `_exit_tree()`, then `NOTIFICATION_PREDELETE`.

Write a script that prints in all five and run it inside a two-level tree. Do it once; the order will stick.
owner, get_parent, $ paths and % unique:
Four ways to get hold of another node, in increasing order of how much you should like them:

· `get_node("Sprite2D")`, written `$Sprite2D` — a path relative to this node. `$Body/Sprite2D` goes down; `$"../Other"` goes up. Fragile: rename the node and it breaks silently at runtime.
· `get_parent()` — works, but a node that reaches *up* is a node that cannot be instanced anywhere else.
· **Unique names** — right-click a node > **Access as Unique Name**. It gets a `%` prefix, and `%Health` finds it anywhere in the scene regardless of depth. Rename-safe for *moves*, and the right default for reaching your own children.
· `@export var target: Node2D` — you assign it by dragging in the Inspector. No path at all, and it cannot silently break.

`owner` is different: it is the root of the *scene file* a node was saved in, not its parent. You need it rarely, but when you are writing `@tool` scripts or saving scenes at runtime, `owner` is the thing that decides what gets written.
Attach a script: extends, class_name, an:
Select a node > the **scroll-with-a-plus icon** in the Scene dock, or right-click > Attach Script. Godot offers a path and a template.

Every script starts with `extends`:

```gdscript
extends Node2D
class_name Player
```

· `extends` says what this script *is*. You get every property, method and signal of that class. Attach a script to a node of an incompatible type and Godot refuses.
· `class_name` registers the script **engine-wide**: `Player` becomes usable as a type annotation anywhere, appears in the Create Node dialog, and gets an icon with `@icon("res://…")`.

Order matters: `@icon`, then `class_name`, then `extends` is the conventional top (Godot accepts `class_name` and `extends` in either order; pick one and be consistent).

Delete the template's commented-out `_ready` and `_process`. An empty `_process` still costs a call every frame.
Variables, static typing, and why you al:
```gdscript
var speed := 220.0          # inferred float
var name: String = "Greg"   # explicit
var target: Node2D          # typed, starts null
```

`:=` infers the type from the value. `: Type` states it. Both give you **static typing**, and you want it on every variable without exception:

· The editor autocompletes properly — untyped, it cannot know what `target` is and offers you nothing.
· Typos become **errors at parse time** instead of silent `null` at 2am.
· Typed GDScript is measurably faster; the compiler can skip variant dispatch.

`var x = 5` with a bare `=` and no annotation is untyped and should feel wrong to write.

Also: `@onready var sprite := $Sprite2D` — `@onready` defers the assignment until `_ready()`, which is the only point `$` paths are safe. Writing `var sprite := $Sprite2D` without it is a null reference every time.
Constants, enums, and static variables:
```gdscript
const MAX_HEALTH := 100
const SPEEDS := {"walk": 90.0, "run": 220.0}

enum State { IDLE, WALK, ATTACK, DEAD }
var state: State = State.IDLE

static var instances := 0
```

· `const` is resolved at parse time and cannot be changed. Use it for every magic number — a `220.0` buried in a movement function is a number you will be hunting in six months.
· `enum` makes a named integer set. `State.WALK` is `1`. It gives you autocomplete, it shows as a **dropdown** in the Inspector when exported, and it makes `match` readable.
· `static var` belongs to the *class*, not the instance — shared by every object of that type. Useful for counters and caches; a trap if you forget it is shared.

`const` can hold a preloaded scene: `const Bullet := preload("res://bullet.tscn")` is the idiomatic way to reference another scene.
Control flow: if, elif, else, and match:
```gdscript
if health <= 0:
    die()
elif health < 20:
    stagger()
else:
    walk()
```

Indentation is the block. Tabs, one level per block, and no braces anywhere.

`match` is the one worth learning properly, because it does more than a switch:

```gdscript
match state:
    State.IDLE:
        pass
    State.WALK, State.RUN:      # multiple patterns
        move()
    var other:                  # binds, acts as default
        push_warning("unhandled %s" % other)
```

It also destructures:

```gdscript
match event_data:
    {"type": "hit", "amount": var n}:
        take_damage(n)
    [x, y]:
        move_to(Vector2(x, y))
```

That dictionary-and-array pattern matching has no equivalent in most languages and is worth reaching for when parsing saved data.
Loops: for, while, range, break and cont:
```gdscript
for i in 10:                      # 0..9, no range() needed
    print(i)

for i in range(2, 10, 2):         # start, stop, step
    print(i)

for enemy in enemies:             # any array
    enemy.alert()

for key in stats:                 # dictionary keys
    print(key, stats[key])

while not is_on_floor():
    await get_tree().physics_frame
```

`for i in 10` iterating 0-9 is a GDScript shorthand worth knowing — `range(10)` is identical but allocates.

`break` leaves the loop, `continue` skips to the next iteration.

The one real trap: **never modify an array while iterating it.** Removing elements shifts the indices under the loop and you will silently skip items. Iterate over a copy (`for e in enemies.duplicate()`) or collect what to remove and do it after.
Functions, default arguments, and return:
```gdscript
func take_damage(amount: int, source: Node = null) -> void:
    health -= amount
    if health <= 0:
        die()

func distance_to_player() -> float:
    return global_position.distance_to(player.global_position)
```

`-> void` and `-> float` are the return annotations. **Always write them** — `-> void` makes "this returns nothing" explicit and the parser catches an accidental `return x`.

Default arguments must come after non-default ones, as everywhere.

Two modifiers:
· `static func` — callable on the class without an instance: `Utils.clamp_angle(a)`. Good for pure maths helpers. It cannot touch instance variables or the tree.
· An underscore prefix (`func _internal()`) is convention, not enforcement. GDScript has no private; the underscore means "do not call this from outside" and is honoured socially.

Functions beginning with a single underscore that Godot itself calls — `_ready`, `_process`, `_input` — are **virtual** methods. You are overriding, not inventing.
Arrays and typed arrays:
```gdscript
var loose := [1, "two", Vector2.ZERO]       # untyped, mixed, avoid
var enemies: Array[Node2D] = []             # typed, do this
```

A typed array rejects the wrong type at runtime and autocompletes its elements. Use it everywhere.

The methods you will actually use:

```gdscript
a.append(x)        a.append_array(b)
a.size()           a.is_empty()
a.has(x)           a.find(x)        # -1 if absent
a.erase(x)         a.remove_at(i)   a.pop_back()
a.sort()           a.sort_custom(func(p, q): return p.hp < q.hp)
a.filter(func(e): return e.alive)
a.map(func(e): return e.name)
a.reduce(func(acc, e): return acc + e.hp, 0)
a.pick_random()    a.shuffle()
a.slice(1, 3)      a.duplicate()
```

`-1` indexes from the end: `a[-1]` is the last element.

And the packed arrays — `PackedVector2Array`, `PackedInt32Array`, `PackedByteArray` — are tightly stored and much cheaper for large homogeneous data. Any engine API that takes many points takes a packed array.
Dictionaries:
```gdscript
var stats := {"hp": 100, "speed": 220.0}
var typed: Dictionary[String, int] = {}     # Godot 4.4+
```

Keys can be any type, including nodes and vectors — `grid[Vector2i(3, 4)]` is a perfectly good sparse tilemap.

```gdscript
stats["hp"] = 90        stats.hp = 90        # both work for String keys
stats.has("hp")
stats.get("mana", 0)    # default instead of an error
stats.erase("hp")
stats.keys()            stats.values()
stats.merge(other, true)   # true = overwrite
```

The trap: reading a missing key with `[]` throws, reading with `.get(key, default)` does not. For anything loaded from disk or built at runtime, use `.get()`.

Dictionaries are **ordered** by insertion in Godot 4, which you can rely on.

And they are **passed by reference**, like arrays. `var copy := stats` gives you a second name for the same dictionary. `stats.duplicate(true)` gives you a real deep copy.
Classes: inner classes, inheritance, and:
A script *is* a class. Beyond that:

```gdscript
class_name Enemy
extends CharacterBody2D

func take_damage(n: int) -> void:
    health -= n
```

```gdscript
class_name Archer
extends Enemy

func take_damage(n: int) -> void:
    super(n)              # run Enemy's version
    flee()
```

`super()` calls the parent's version of the method you are in; `super.other_method()` calls a different one. Omit it and you have *replaced* the parent's behaviour, which is sometimes what you want and usually a bug.

Inner classes, for small data holders that do not deserve a file:

```gdscript
class Shot:
    var at: Vector2
    var power: float
    func _init(a: Vector2, p: float) -> void:
        at = a
        power = p

var s := Shot.new(Vector2.ZERO, 3.0)
```

For data that should be **editable in the Inspector or saved to disk**, use a `Resource` instead — stage 7. Inner classes cannot do either.
_process and _physics_process, and what:
```gdscript
func _process(delta: float) -> void:
    rotation += 2.0 * delta

func _physics_process(delta: float) -> void:
    velocity.y += gravity * delta
    move_and_slide()
```

· `_process` runs **once per rendered frame** — 60, 144, or 300 times a second depending on the machine. `delta` is the actual seconds since the last frame and varies.
· `_physics_process` runs at a **fixed rate**, 60 Hz by default (Project Settings > Physics > Common > Physics Ticks per Second). `delta` is almost always exactly `1.0/60.0`.

The rule: **anything involving physics bodies, collision or movement goes in `_physics_process`.** Visual-only work — rotating a decoration, lerping a camera, updating a label — goes in `_process`.

`delta` exists so behaviour is frame-rate independent. `position.x += 5` moves five times faster at 300 fps than at 60. `position.x += 300 * delta` moves 300 pixels per second on any machine. Multiplying by `delta` is not optional and forgetting it is the most common movement bug there is.

The exception that catches everyone: `lerp(a, b, 0.1)` in `_process` is *not* frame-rate independent either. Use `lerp(a, b, 1.0 - exp(-rate * delta))`, or `a.move_toward(b, speed * delta)`.

If you do not need per-frame work, delete the function. `set_process(false)` turns it off at runtime.
Callable, lambdas, and bind:
A `Callable` is a reference to a function you can store, pass and call later. Signals are built on it.

```gdscript
var f := move_to          # a method of this object, not called
f.call(Vector2.ZERO)

var g := func(n: int) -> int: return n * 2     # lambda
print(g.call(21))

button.pressed.connect(_on_pressed)
button.pressed.connect(func(): print("hi"))
```

`bind()` pre-fills the **last** arguments, which is how you connect one handler to many senders:

```gdscript
for i in 3:
    buttons[i].pressed.connect(_on_slot_pressed.bind(i))

func _on_slot_pressed(slot: int) -> void:
    print("slot ", slot)
```

`callv(array)` calls with an array of arguments. `is_valid()` tells you whether the target object still exists — a `Callable` does not keep a node alive, and calling into a freed node is an error.

Lambdas capture surrounding variables **by value** at creation. A lambda made inside a loop captures that iteration's value, which is usually what you want and occasionally a surprise.
Node2D: position, rotation, scale, local:
`Node2D` is the base of everything in 2D. Its transform is the whole of it:

· `position` — relative to the **parent**. `global_position` — relative to the world.
· `rotation` in **radians**; `rotation_degrees` if you prefer. `deg_to_rad()` and `rad_to_deg()` convert.
· `scale` — multiply. Scaling a parent scales children, including their collision shapes, which is a common source of mysterious physics.
· `z_index` — draw order within the same parent, -4096 to 4096. `z_as_relative` (default on) makes it relative to the parent's.

The child-of-a-rotated-parent rule: set `position` on a child and you are working in the parent's rotated, scaled space. Set `global_position` and you are working in world space. Mixing them up produces movement that drifts when the parent turns.

Useful transform helpers: `look_at(point)`, `rotate(angle)`, `translate(offset)`, `to_local(global_point)`, `to_global(local_point)`, and `global_transform` if you need the whole matrix.

`Vector2` basics worth memorising: `.length()`, `.normalized()`, `.angle()`, `.rotated(a)`, `.distance_to(b)`, `.dot(b)`, `.lerp(b, t)`, `Vector2.ZERO/ONE/UP/RIGHT`. In Godot 2D, **+Y is down** and `Vector2.UP` is `(0, -1)`.
Sprite2D, texture import, and turning fi:
`Sprite2D` draws a `Texture2D`. The properties that matter:

· `texture` — drag a PNG in.
· `centered` — on by default, so the node's origin is the sprite's middle. For a character whose feet should be the origin, turn it off and set `offset` to `(-w/2, -h)`.
· `flip_h` / `flip_v` — cheaper and simpler than a negative scale.
· `region_enabled` + `region_rect` — draw one rectangle out of a sheet.
· `hframes` / `vframes` + `frame` — treat the texture as a grid and pick a cell. This is the cheap way to use a sprite sheet without an `AnimatedSprite2D`.

**Filtering.** Select the PNG in FileSystem > **Import** dock > set **Filter** off, then **Reimport**. Or set it once for the whole project: Project Settings > Rendering > Textures > Canvas Textures > Default Texture Filter = **Nearest**.

Do this before you draw anything. Linear filtering on pixel art produces soft, wrong edges, and it is the default.
Input: the InputMap, is_action_pressed a:
**Project > Project Settings > Input Map.** Type an action name, Add, then click `+` to bind keys, mouse buttons, or gamepad inputs. Several bindings per action is the point — keyboard and gamepad feed the same action.

Never check for a raw key in gameplay code. `Input.is_key_pressed(KEY_W)` cannot be rebound; `Input.is_action_pressed("move_up")` can.

The three you need, and the difference is the whole lesson:

```gdscript
Input.is_action_pressed("jump")        # true every frame it is held
Input.is_action_just_pressed("jump")   # true on the one frame it went down
Input.is_action_just_released("jump")  # true on the one frame it came up
```

Hold for continuous things, `just_pressed` for discrete things. A jump on `is_action_pressed` jumps every frame you hold the key.

For movement, two helpers that replace four `if`s:

```gdscript
var dir := Input.get_axis("move_left", "move_right")        # -1..1
var move := Input.get_vector("left", "right", "up", "down") # Vector2, deadzoned
```

`get_vector` handles analogue sticks and normalises diagonals. Writing it by hand gets diagonal movement wrong by a factor of 1.414, which is the oldest bug in games.
_input, _unhandled_input, and the event:
Polling with `Input.is_action_pressed` is for *states*. For *events* — a keypress, a click, a mouse motion — override a callback and you get each event exactly once:

```gdscript
func _unhandled_input(event: InputEvent) -> void:
    if event.is_action_pressed("interact"):
        interact()
    elif event is InputEventMouseButton and event.pressed:
        shoot_at(get_global_mouse_position())
```

The order an event travels, which is the part worth knowing:

1. `_input()` on every node, **reverse tree order** — last child first.
2. **GUI** — `Control` nodes get `_gui_input()`, and a Control that handles a click consumes it.
3. `_shortcut_input()`, then `_unhandled_key_input()`, then `_unhandled_input()`.

So **gameplay belongs in `_unhandled_input`**: by the time it fires, the UI has had its chance, and a click on a button does not also fire your gun. That one choice removes a whole category of bug.

`get_viewport().set_input_as_handled()` stops an event travelling further. `event.is_echo()` is true for OS key-repeat, which you almost always want to ignore.
CharacterBody2D and move_and_slide:
The node for anything player- or AI-controlled. Not `RigidBody2D` — you want to say exactly where it goes.

```gdscript
extends CharacterBody2D

@export var speed := 220.0

func _physics_process(delta: float) -> void:
    var dir := Input.get_vector("left", "right", "up", "down")
    velocity = dir * speed
    move_and_slide()
```

`velocity` is a property of the node, in **pixels per second**. `move_and_slide()` reads it, moves, resolves collisions by sliding along surfaces, and writes `velocity` back with the blocked component removed. No `delta` — it applies it internally.

Properties on the node:
· `motion_mode` — **Grounded** for platformers (gravity, floors, `is_on_floor()`), **Floating** for top-down. Set it to Floating for a top-down game or you will fight phantom floor logic.
· `floor_max_angle`, `floor_snap_length`, `up_direction` — platformer slope behaviour.
· `slide_on_ceiling`, `max_slides`.

Collision results: `is_on_floor()`, `is_on_wall()`, `is_on_ceiling()`, `get_wall_normal()`, and `get_slide_collision_count()` / `get_slide_collision(i)` to find out *what* you hit.

`move_and_collide(motion)` is the lower-level alternative: it moves once, stops at the first contact, and hands you the `KinematicCollision2D`. Use it when you want to decide what happens rather than slide.
CollisionShape2D, and choosing the shape:
A physics body does nothing without a shape. Add a `CollisionShape2D` child, then in the Inspector create a **Shape** resource:

· `RectangleShape2D` — cheapest and most predictable. Default choice.
· `CircleShape2D` — cheapest of all, and it never catches on corners. Best for anything that moves fast or slides along walls.
· `CapsuleShape2D` — a character standing up.
· `SegmentShape2D`, `WorldBoundaryShape2D` — thin walls, infinite floors.
· `ConvexPolygonShape2D` — custom, still fast.
· `ConcavePolygonShape2D` — arbitrary, **slow, and not reliable for moving bodies**. Static geometry only.

Rules of thumb that save hours: one shape per body wherever possible; several `CollisionShape2D` children of one body is fine and cheaper than several bodies; and **never scale a collision shape via the node's `scale`** — resize the shape resource instead. Scaled shapes behave subtly wrong.

Turn on **Debug > Visible Collision Shapes** in the editor menu and leave it on while building. Running with shapes drawn is how you find out the shape is not where you think it is.

And a shape resource dragged into two nodes is **shared**: resizing one resizes both. Click the resource and **Make Unique** when that is not what you want.
Area2D, body_entered, and overlap querie:
`Area2D` detects rather than blocks. Hitboxes, pickups, triggers, damage zones, detection radii — all `Area2D`.

Its signals, connected in the **Node dock**:

```gdscript
func _on_body_entered(body: Node2D) -> void:
    if body is Player:
        body.take_damage(damage)
        queue_free()
```

· `body_entered` / `body_exited` — physics **bodies** (CharacterBody2D, RigidBody2D, StaticBody2D).
· `area_entered` / `area_exited` — other **Areas**. Hitbox-meets-hurtbox is area-to-area.
· `mouse_entered` / `mouse_exited` / `input_event`.

Polling instead of signalling, when you need the current state rather than the moment of change:

```gdscript
for body in area.get_overlapping_bodies():
    body.push(direction)
```

Two things that bite. First, `monitoring` and `monitorable` are separate: `monitoring` means this area detects others, `monitorable` means others can detect it. Turn `monitoring` off on a pure hurtbox and save the work.

Second, **overlap state updates on the physics tick, not immediately.** An area moved or enabled this frame reports nothing until `await get_tree().physics_frame`. Spawning a hitbox and querying overlaps in the same frame returns empty, every time.
RigidBody2D and StaticBody2D — when each:
Four body types, and picking the wrong one is a week of fighting the engine:

· **StaticBody2D** — does not move. Walls, floors, scenery. Cheapest. It can still have a `constant_linear_velocity` to act as a conveyor.
· **CharacterBody2D** — you move it, in code, with `move_and_slide()`. Players and most enemies. Full control, no physics realism.
· **RigidBody2D** — the **physics engine** moves it. You apply forces and impulses, not positions. Crates, debris, ragdolls, anything that should tumble.
· **AnimatableBody2D** — moved by animation or code, but it *pushes* rigid bodies correctly. Moving platforms and doors.

For `RigidBody2D`, the rule that is not obvious: **never set `position` directly.** It fights the solver and produces jitter. Use `apply_central_impulse()`, `apply_force()`, or set `linear_velocity`. If you must teleport it, do it inside `_integrate_forces(state)` via `state.transform`.

Its `freeze` + `freeze_mode` lets you park one cheaply. `gravity_scale = 0` makes a floating object that still collides and tumbles.

Mixing a `CharacterBody2D` into a pile of rigid bodies does not push them by default — a kinematic body has infinite mass. Detect the collision via `get_slide_collision(i)` and apply an impulse yourself.
Built-in signals, and connecting them in:
Select a node, open the **Node** dock (tabbed beside the Inspector), **Signals**. Every signal the node emits is listed.

Double-click one > pick the node that should receive it > Connect. Godot writes the method into that node's script and puts a small green **connection icon** beside the emitter in the Scene dock.

Signals you will use constantly: `Button.pressed`, `Timer.timeout`, `Area2D.body_entered`, `AnimationPlayer.animation_finished`, `AnimatedSprite2D.animation_finished`, `Tree.item_selected`, and `get_tree().node_added`.

The editor connection is stored **in the `.tscn`**, which has one real consequence: a connection you cannot find in any script is in the scene file. When tracing "what calls this", search the `.tscn` as well as the `.gd`.

Editor-connected or code-connected is a genuine choice. Editor is visible in the Scene dock and survives refactoring badly; code is greppable and explicit. The usual convention: connect in the editor for UI inside one scene, connect in code for anything instanced at runtime.
Declaring signals, and emitting them:
```gdscript
signal died
signal health_changed(current: int, maximum: int)

func take_damage(n: int) -> void:
    health -= n
    health_changed.emit(health, max_health)
    if health <= 0:
        died.emit()
```

A declared signal becomes a property of the object. `health_changed.emit(...)` is the Godot 4 way; `emit_signal("health_changed", ...)` still works, is string-based, and gives you no error if you typo the name — do not use it.

Type the arguments. An untyped signal argument is an untyped variable in every handler.

What a signal buys you: the node that emits it **does not know who is listening**. The health bar, the screen-shake, the achievement tracker and the save system can all connect to `health_changed`, and the health script never mentions any of them. Add a fifth listener and the emitter does not change.

Emitting into nothing is free and legal. A signal with no connections costs a dictionary lookup.
connect() in code, and disconnecting:
```gdscript
enemy.died.connect(_on_enemy_died)
enemy.died.connect(_on_enemy_died.bind(enemy))      # pass the sender
enemy.died.connect(func(): score += 10)             # lambda
```

Flags, as the fourth argument:

```gdscript
enemy.died.connect(_on_died, CONNECT_ONE_SHOT)   # disconnects itself after firing
enemy.died.connect(_on_died, CONNECT_DEFERRED)   # fires at idle time, not now
```

`CONNECT_ONE_SHOT` is the clean way to handle "the first time only" without a boolean.

Housekeeping: `is_connected(sig, callable)` before connecting if a path might run twice — connecting the same callable twice means the handler runs twice, and Godot warns but does not stop you. `disconnect(sig, callable)` to undo.

You rarely need to disconnect manually. A connection where **either** object is freed is dropped automatically. Where it does matter: connecting a long-lived autoload's method to a short-lived node's signal is fine, but connecting a *node's* method to an *autoload's* signal leaks logically — the autoload outlives the node, and while Godot cleans the connection up, any `CONNECT_PERSIST` or re-entry assumptions will not hold.
Who connects to whom: call down, signal:
The structural rule that keeps a Godot project from becoming a knot. There is only one:

**A node may call its children. A node may not call its parent — it emits a signal and lets the parent decide.**

So:
· `Player` calls `$Sprite.play("run")`. Fine — downward.
· `Player` wants the HUD updated. It **does not** call `get_parent().get_node("HUD")`. It emits `health_changed` and the scene that owns both wires them together.

Why it matters practically: a node that reaches upward or sideways with `get_parent()` or `$"../../Thing"` can only ever live in exactly that tree position. Move it, instance it somewhere else, or test it alone with `F6`, and it crashes. A node that only signals upward can be dropped anywhere.

The connecting happens at the level that **owns both** — usually the scene root, in its `_ready()`:

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
    player.health_changed.connect(hud.set_health)
    player.died.connect(_on_player_died)
```

Read that `_ready()` and you can see the whole scene's wiring in one place. That is the payoff.
Groups: add_to_group, and when that is t:
A group is a string tag on a node. Set it in the **Node dock > Groups**, or in code:

```gdscript
add_to_group("enemies")
remove_from_group("enemies")
is_in_group("enemies")
```

Then reach the whole set without holding references:

```gdscript
for e in get_tree().get_nodes_in_group("enemies"):
    e.alert(global_position)

get_tree().call_group("enemies", "alert", global_position)
get_tree().get_first_node_in_group("player")
```

`call_group` is fire-and-forget: nodes without that method are skipped silently, which is convenient and hides typos.

When a group is right: a set with no natural owner, whose membership changes at runtime — all enemies, all save-able objects, everything that should pause. `get_first_node_in_group("player")` is also the least-bad way for a wandering node to find the player.

When it is wrong: as a substitute for a reference you already have, or as a type check. `if node.is_in_group("enemy")` works, but `if node is Enemy` is checked by the compiler and cannot be misspelled.

`get_nodes_in_group` builds an array every call. In `_process` over hundreds of nodes, cache it.
Autoloads: what earns one, and what does:
**Project Settings > Globals > Autoload.** Point it at a script or a scene, give it a name, and Godot instances it once at startup as a child of the root — reachable from anywhere by that name:

```gdscript
Game.score += 10
Audio.play_sfx("hit")
```

Autoloads are above every scene, so they survive `change_scene_to_file()`. That is their real purpose.

What genuinely earns one:
· The **save system** — one owner of the file.
· **Audio** — one place that holds buses and plays one-shots.
· **Scene transitions** — the thing that fades out, swaps the scene, fades in. It cannot live in a scene it is replacing.
· A **global event bus** — an object that only declares signals, so unrelated systems can talk without knowing each other.

What does not: anything one scene could own. Every autoload is global mutable state, it is initialised in a fixed order you must then reason about, it makes any scene depend invisibly on it, and it cannot be tested in isolation. Four or five is a healthy project; twenty means the scene tree is not being used.

The order in that list is the initialisation order, and an autoload's `_ready()` cannot assume a later one exists.
queue_free, free, and is_instance_valid:
```gdscript
node.queue_free()    # deleted at the end of the frame
node.free()          # deleted right now
```

**Use `queue_free()`.** `free()` deletes the object mid-frame while the engine, the physics server and your own loops may still be holding it, and that is a crash. The only safe `free()` is on an object not in the tree.

What `queue_free()` does: marks the node, finishes the frame, then removes it and **every descendant**, firing `_exit_tree()` and `NOTIFICATION_PREDELETE`. Between the call and the deletion the node is still there and still processing — guard with `is_queued_for_deletion()` if that matters.

After it is gone, any variable still pointing at it holds a **freed object**, and touching it errors. Check:

```gdscript
if is_instance_valid(target):
    target.hit()
```

`if target:` is **not** enough — a freed object is not null, and in a release build the check passes and then crashes.

The alternatives to deletion: `remove_child()` takes a node out of the tree and hands you ownership (you must then free it or re-add it, or it leaks). `hide()` plus `set_process(false)` keeps a node for reuse, which is the basis of object pooling for bullets.

`get_tree().queue_delete(node)` does not exist; `queue_free()` is a method on the node.
await, and awaiting a signal:
`await` suspends the function until something happens, and resumes it in place. It makes sequences readable:

```gdscript
func open_chest() -> void:
    anim.play("open")
    await anim.animation_finished
    spawn_loot()
    await get_tree().create_timer(0.5).timeout
    play_jingle()
```

Two forms:
· `await some_signal` — waits for that signal; evaluates to its arguments.
· `await some_function()` — waits for a function that itself awaits (a coroutine).

The frame-waiting idioms you will need constantly:

```gdscript
await get_tree().process_frame      # next rendered frame
await get_tree().physics_frame      # next physics tick
```

Those two solve the "it is not ready yet in the same frame" class of problem — a freshly added node, a freshly moved area, a freshly baked navigation map.

Three traps. A function containing `await` returns immediately with a `Signal`-like value, so **its caller gets nothing useful** unless the caller awaits too. If the awaited signal never fires, the function never resumes and there is no error. And if the node is freed while suspended, the resumption is dropped — so after any `await`, re-check `is_instance_valid()` before touching things you cached before it.
AnimatedSprite2D and SpriteFrames:
`AnimatedSprite2D` plays named flipbook animations. Its `sprite_frames` property holds a **SpriteFrames** resource, and clicking it opens the **SpriteFrames editor** in the bottom panel.

In that panel: animations down the left, frames along the bottom. Per animation you set **Speed (FPS)** and **Loop**. The animation named `default` exists until you rename it.

```gdscript
anim.play("run")
anim.play("idle")
anim.stop()
anim.pause()
anim.frame = 0
anim.speed_scale = 1.5          # multiplies the animation's own FPS
anim.flip_h = velocity.x < 0
```

`animation_finished` fires only on non-looping animations. `frame_changed` fires on every frame, which is how you put a footstep sound on frames 2 and 6.

Calling `play("run")` when `"run"` is already playing is a no-op — it does *not* restart. To restart deliberately: `anim.frame = 0` first, or `play()` a different animation.

Save the `SpriteFrames` as its own `.tres` file rather than leaving it embedded in the scene. Then several scenes can share it, and it diffs separately in git.
Importing a sprite sheet into SpriteFram:
In the SpriteFrames editor, the toolbar above the frame strip has two **Add frames** buttons:

· **Add frames from sprite sheet** — pick the PNG, then set **Horizontal** and **Vertical** cell counts. The grid overlays the image; click or drag-select the cells for this animation, in order, and Add. Select them in the wrong order and the animation plays in the wrong order.
· **Add frames from file** — one PNG per frame.

The dialog also offers **Size**, **Separation** and **Offset** for sheets with padding between cells.

Do each animation as its own pass: create the animation, name it (`idle`, `run`, `attack` — lower-case snake case, consistently), then select just that row of cells.

For an 8-direction character this becomes 8 animations per action, named systematically: `run_n`, `run_ne`, `run_e`, and so on. Name them so they can be built from code — `anim.play("run_" + dir_name)` is the whole direction system, and it only works if the naming is mechanical.
AnimationPlayer: keyframe any property,:
This is the one that changes what you can build. `AnimationPlayer` animates **any property of any node** in the scene, over time, on a timeline.

Add the node, open the **Animation** bottom panel, **Animation > New**, name it, set its length and whether it loops.

To add a track: select a node in the Scene dock, find the property in the Inspector, and click the **key icon** beside it. Godot creates the track and inserts a keyframe at the playhead. Move the playhead, change the value, key again.

So you can animate `position`, `rotation`, `modulate`, `scale`, a shader parameter, a `Light2D`'s energy, a Label's text, or a custom `@export` variable on your own script — all in one animation.

Controls: `Ctrl+Click` on the timeline to move the playhead, the **snap** field at the top-right (set it to 0.1 or 1/60), and the per-key **Update Mode** (Continuous / Discrete / Capture) which decides whether values interpolate or jump.

```gdscript
player.play("attack")
player.play_backwards("open")
player.current_animation_position
player.speed_scale = 2.0
await player.animation_finished
```

Save animations into an `AnimationLibrary` `.tres` when more than one scene needs them.
Tracks: property, call-method, audio, an:
The **Add Track** button offers more than property tracks, and the other kinds are the useful part:

· **Property Track** — the default. Interpolates a value.
· **Call Method Track** — calls a method on a node at a point in time, with arguments. Right-click the track at a time > Insert Key > pick the method. This is how a 12-frame attack deals damage on frame 5: the animation calls `_enable_hitbox()` then `_disable_hitbox()`. The timing lives with the art instead of in a `Timer`.
· **Audio Playback Track** — drop an `AudioStream` on a timeline position, routed through an `AudioStreamPlayer`. Footsteps and swings, placed visually.
· **Animation Track** — drives *another* `AnimationPlayer`. Good for cutscenes composed of per-object animations.
· **Bezier Track** — a property with hand-drawn curves rather than ease presets. For motion that needs to feel exactly right.

Per-track, the right-hand buttons set the **interpolation** (Nearest / Linear / Cubic) and the **loop wrap**. Nearest on a `frame` property is how you hand-animate a sprite sheet inside `AnimationPlayer` instead of `AnimatedSprite2D` — which is worth doing when the animation also needs to move the body and fire a hitbox.
animation_finished, animation_changed, a:
```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
    anim.animation_finished.connect(_on_anim_finished)

func _on_anim_finished(name: StringName) -> void:
    match name:
        "attack":
            state = State.IDLE
        "die":
            queue_free()
```

`animation_finished` passes the animation **name**, which is what lets one handler serve the whole node. It does **not** fire for looping animations — a looping animation never finishes.

Other signals: `animation_changed(old, new)`, `animation_started(name)`, and `current_animation_changed(name)`.

The pattern this enables, and it is worth internalising before stage 6's state machines: an attack is not "play the animation, start a 0.4-second timer, hope they match". It is "play the animation, await its end". Change the animation's length later and the code still works, because there is only one source of truth for how long an attack takes.

```gdscript
func attack() -> void:
    state = State.ATTACK
    anim.play("attack")
    await anim.animation_finished
    if is_instance_valid(self):
        state = State.IDLE
```
AnimationTree and the StateMachine node:
`AnimationPlayer` plays one animation. `AnimationTree` decides **which** animation and blends between them, and it is the standard answer to "my character script is 300 lines of `play()` calls".

Setup: add an `AnimationTree`, set `anim_player` to your `AnimationPlayer`, set `tree_root` to a new **AnimationNodeStateMachine**, and turn `active` on.

Click the tree root and the bottom panel becomes a **graph editor**. Right-click to add nodes:
· **Animation** — plays one clip from the player.
· **StateMachine** — nested, for sub-states.
· **BlendSpace1D / 2D**, **Blend2 / Blend3**, **OneShot**, **TimeScale**, **Transition**.

Draw a transition by dragging from one node to another. Select the arrow and set:
· **Switch Mode** — Immediate / Sync / **At End**. "At End" is how an attack finishes before idle takes over.
· **Advance Mode** — Disabled / Enabled / **Auto**. Auto transitions fire by themselves when the condition passes.
· **Advance Condition** — the name of a boolean parameter. Set it from code and the machine moves itself.
· **Xfade Time** — crossfade seconds.

The `Start` and `End` nodes are automatic. A transition from `Any` state is drawn from the special `Any` input, which is how `die` interrupts everything.
travel(), and the playback parameter:
The `AnimationTree`'s state machine is driven through a playback object, fetched by a string path:

```gdscript
@onready var tree: AnimationTree = $AnimationTree
@onready var sm: AnimationNodeStateMachinePlayback = tree["parameters/playback"]

sm.travel("attack")
```

`travel()` is the important one: it does not jump: it finds the **shortest path of transitions** from the current state to the one you asked for, and walks it, respecting each transition's switch mode and crossfade. Ask for `attack` from `run` and it goes `run → attack` if that arrow exists.

`sm.start("idle")` jumps immediately, ignoring transitions. `sm.stop()`. `sm.get_current_node()` tells you where it is. `sm.travel_to_end()`.

Every other parameter is set the same way, by path:

```gdscript
tree.set("parameters/conditions/is_moving", velocity.length() > 5.0)
tree.set("parameters/Walk/blend_position", direction)
tree.set("parameters/Shoot/request", AnimationNodeOneShot.ONE_SHOT_REQUEST_FIRE)
```

Those strings are visible in the Inspector under the AnimationTree's **Parameters** section once the tree is built, which is how you discover them rather than guessing.

The payoff: the character script sets a handful of booleans and a direction vector, and the graph decides what plays. The 300 lines go away.
BlendSpace2D for 8-direction movement:
Add an **AnimationNodeBlendSpace2D** inside the state machine and open it. You get a 2D field; drag animations from the `AnimationPlayer` list onto points in it.

For an 8-direction character: place `run_n` at (0, -1), `run_e` at (1, 0), `run_s` at (0, 1), `run_w` at (-1, 0), and the diagonals at the corners — matching `Vector2`'s convention where **+Y is down**.

Then set the blend position to the direction you are moving:

```gdscript
tree.set("parameters/Run/blend_position", velocity.normalized())
```

And the correct clip plays, chosen by proximity.

The setting that matters for pixel art: the toolbar's **Blend** mode. The default **Interpolated** cross-fades between neighbouring clips, which on pixel sprites produces a ghosted double image. Switch it to **Discrete** — snap to the nearest point, no blending — or **Carry**, which snaps but preserves the playback position so the legs do not reset mid-stride. **Carry** is usually what an 8-direction pixel character wants.

A `BlendSpace1D` does the same on one axis, which is the right tool for a speed blend from walk through jog to run.
Tween: create_tween, tween_property, and:
A `Tween` animates a value in code, with no node and no timeline. For UI motion, juice, and anything procedural it beats `AnimationPlayer` outright.

```gdscript
var t := create_tween()
t.tween_property(self, "position", target, 0.4)
```

`create_tween()` is a method on any `Node`; the tween is bound to that node and dies with it. **Tweens are one-shot** — you create a fresh one each time, you do not keep one around.

Chaining, which is the whole point:

```gdscript
var t := create_tween()
t.set_trans(Tween.TRANS_BACK).set_ease(Tween.EASE_OUT)
t.tween_property(sprite, "scale", Vector2(1.3, 0.7), 0.1)
t.tween_property(sprite, "scale", Vector2.ONE, 0.25)
t.tween_callback(func(): hitbox.monitoring = true)
t.tween_interval(0.2)
t.tween_property(self, "modulate:a", 0.0, 0.3)
```

Steps run **in sequence** by default; `t.set_parallel()` makes them simultaneous, and `t.chain()` returns to sequence. Note `"modulate:a"` — a colon addresses a **sub-property**, so you can tween just the alpha or just `position:x`.

Other methods: `tween_method(callable, from, to, time)` for a value with no property to hold it; `set_loops()`; `set_speed_scale()`; `kill()`; `await t.finished`.

Transitions worth knowing by feel: `TRANS_SINE` for gentle, `TRANS_CUBIC` for standard, `TRANS_BACK` for overshoot, `TRANS_ELASTIC` for bounce, `TRANS_EXPO` for snap.
Timer, create_timer, and counting frames:
Three ways to wait, and each is right somewhere:

**A `Timer` node** — for a repeating or restartable wait that belongs to the scene:

```gdscript
$Cooldown.wait_time = 1.5
$Cooldown.one_shot = true
$Cooldown.start()
await $Cooldown.timeout
```

`autostart`, `one_shot`, and `paused` are Inspector properties. `time_left` reads the remainder, which is what you bind a cooldown ring to. Restarting is `start()`, and it is the only one of the three you can cancel or query.

**A one-off timer with no node:**

```gdscript
await get_tree().create_timer(0.5).timeout
```

Perfect for a one-time delay inside a sequence. It cannot be cancelled, and if the node is freed while waiting the continuation is silently dropped — so re-check `is_instance_valid(self)` after it.

**Counting in `_physics_process`** — when the wait must be deterministic and inspectable:

```gdscript
cooldown = maxf(cooldown - delta, 0.0)
if cooldown == 0.0 and Input.is_action_pressed("shoot"):
    shoot()
    cooldown = fire_rate
```

This is the one to use for anything gameplay-critical and frequently queried. A float on the object is cheaper than a node, it survives save/load trivially, and you can see its value in the remote inspector.
Saving a .tres, and editing it in the In:
Three ways to make one:

· **FileSystem dock > right-click > New Resource**, search your `class_name`, save as `res://data/enemies/archer.tres`.
· In the Inspector on an `@export var stats: StatBlock` slot, click the dropdown > **New StatBlock**, fill it in, then the **save icon** > Save As to give it a file.
· In code: `var s := StatBlock.new()` then `ResourceSaver.save(s, path)`.

Open the `.tres` in a text editor — it is the same format as a `.tscn`:

```
[gd_resource type="Resource" script_class="StatBlock" load_steps=2 format=3]

[ext_resource type="Script" path="res://data/stat_block.gd" id="1"]

[resource]
script = ExtResource("1")
display_name = "Archer"
max_health = 60
```

Plain text, diffs in git, editable by hand or by script. `.res` is the binary equivalent — smaller and faster to load, unreadable in a diff. Use `.tres` for anything you author, `.res` for anything generated.

The practical payoff: twenty enemies become twenty `.tres` files in a folder, authored in the Inspector, with one script and one scene. That is the shape a Godot project should have.
The shared-resource trap: duplicate() an:
The bug every Godot project hits once. A `Resource` loaded from a path is **one object shared by every holder**:

```gdscript
@export var stats: StatBlock

func take_damage(n: int) -> void:
    stats.max_health -= n       # WRONG — every archer in the game just changed
```

Twenty archers share one `archer.tres`. Writing to it writes to all of them, and because `.tres` is a file, in the editor it can even be saved to disk.

Three fixes, in order of preference:

**1. Keep resources read-only.** Copy the values into the node's own variables in `_ready()`. The resource is the *template*; the node holds the *state*.

```gdscript
var health: int

func _ready() -> void:
    health = stats.max_health
```

**2. `duplicate()`** when the node genuinely needs its own mutable copy:

```gdscript
stats = stats.duplicate(true)      # true = deep, also copies nested resources
```

**3. `resource_local_to_scene = true`** on the resource — the engine then gives each instancing scene its own copy automatically. Convenient, and easy to forget is on.

The same applies to `Shape2D`, `SpriteFrames`, `Material` and `Curve`. "Make Unique" in the Inspector's resource dropdown is the editor's version of `duplicate()`.
preload, load, and ResourceLoader thread:
```gdscript
const Bullet := preload("res://bullet.tscn")      # parse time
var scene := load("res://bullet.tscn")            # run time
```

· `preload()` resolves when the **script is parsed**, before anything runs. The path must be a constant. The resource is in memory before your first frame, and a bad path is a parse error you see immediately.
· `load()` resolves when the line runs, takes a variable path, and returns `null` on failure. It **blocks** — a big scene loaded in `_process` is a visible hitch.

Both are cached: the second `load()` of the same path returns the same object without touching disk.

For anything large, load it off the main thread:

```gdscript
ResourceLoader.load_threaded_request(path)

# then, each frame:
var progress := []
match ResourceLoader.load_threaded_get_status(path, progress):
    ResourceLoader.THREAD_LOAD_IN_PROGRESS:
        bar.value = progress[0]           # 0.0 .. 1.0
    ResourceLoader.THREAD_LOAD_LOADED:
        var res := ResourceLoader.load_threaded_get(path)
    ResourceLoader.THREAD_LOAD_FAILED:
        push_error("failed: " + path)
```

That is how a loading screen works. `progress` must be an empty array you pass in; the status call fills it.

The rule of thumb: `preload` for things used immediately and always, `load` for things chosen at runtime, threaded for level-sized things. Hundreds of `preload`s in a project means a longer startup and a larger resident set — worth knowing, rarely worth fixing.
JSON, and when to use it instead:
```gdscript
var text := JSON.stringify(data, "\t")        # second arg indents

var json := JSON.new()
if json.parse(text) != OK:
    push_error("line %d: %s" % [json.get_error_line(), json.get_error_message()])
else:
    var data: Variant = json.data
```

`JSON.parse_string(text)` is the shortcut, returning `null` on failure with no error detail — fine for data you wrote, not for data a user might edit.

What JSON costs you, and it is the whole decision: **all numbers come back as `float`**, so an `int` saved as `3` returns `3.0`; `Vector2`, `Color` and `Resource` are not representable and must be converted by hand; and dictionary key order is not guaranteed by the format.

So: `store_var` for save games — it round-trips Godot types exactly and needs no conversion layer. JSON for anything that crosses a boundary: a config file a player edits, data from a web API, a level exported from an external tool, something a build script generates.

`ConfigFile` is the third option and the right one for settings:

```gdscript
var cfg := ConfigFile.new()
cfg.set_value("video", "fullscreen", true)
cfg.save("user://settings.cfg")

cfg.load("user://settings.cfg")
var fs: bool = cfg.get_value("video", "fullscreen", false)
```

It is an INI file, it is human-editable, sections keep it tidy, and `get_value` takes a default — so a missing key is not a crash.
@tool scripts: running code in the edito:
Put `@tool` on the first line and the script runs **in the editor**, not just in the game.

```gdscript
@tool
extends Node2D

@export var radius := 64.0:
    set(value):
        radius = value
        queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
    draw_arc(Vector2.ZERO, radius, 0, TAU, 32, Color.YELLOW, 1.0)
```

Now the detection radius is visible in the editor while you place the enemy. That is the point of `@tool`: authoring feedback.

What it is good for — drawing gizmos, generating child nodes from a parameter, validating a scene and calling `push_warning`, keeping two properties in sync, and `_get_configuration_warnings()` which puts a yellow triangle on the node in the Scene dock.

The three rules, because `@tool` bugs are editor crashes:

1. **Guard anything that should only happen at runtime** with `if Engine.is_editor_hint(): return`. Your `_ready()` now runs in the editor too.
2. **An error crashes the editor**, not the game. There is no safe `null` here. Save before testing a tool script.
3. **Do not write to disk or free nodes** casually from a tool script. Adding children in the editor needs `add_child(n)` then `n.owner = get_tree().edited_scene_root` or they will not be saved.

`EditorPlugin` is the next level up — custom docks, bottom panels, inspector widgets and import plugins, registered from `addons/<name>/plugin.cfg` and enabled in Project Settings > Plugins. Worth knowing exists; worth reaching for only when a `@tool` script is not enough.
TileSet and TileMapLayer:
Two objects, and keeping them straight is most of the battle:

· A **TileSet** is a *resource*: the catalogue of tiles, their size, their collision, their terrains. It is data.
· A **TileMapLayer** is a *node*: a grid of cells, each referencing a tile from a TileSet. It is the painted map.

Note **TileMapLayer**, not `TileMap`. The old single `TileMap` node with layers inside it is deprecated as of Godot 4.3 — you now use one `TileMapLayer` node per layer, as siblings, which means each layer has its own transform, visibility, z-index, material and script. Any tutorial showing a `TileMap` node with a Layers array is out of date.

Add a `TileMapLayer`, then in the Inspector create a **New TileSet** on its `tile_set` property. Set the TileSet's **Tile Size** — 16×16 or 32×32, matching your art — before adding anything, because changing it later re-slices everything.

Bottom panel gets two tabs: **TileSet** (define tiles) and **TileMap** (paint them). You will be moving between those two constantly.

In code:

```gdscript
layer.set_cell(Vector2i(3, 4), source_id, atlas_coords)
layer.get_cell_source_id(Vector2i(3, 4))      # -1 if empty
layer.erase_cell(Vector2i(3, 4))
layer.local_to_map(local_pos)
layer.map_to_local(Vector2i(3, 4))            # centre of that cell
layer.get_used_cells()
layer.get_used_rect()
```
Atlas sources, and painting a map:
In the **TileSet** tab, the left panel lists **sources**. Click `+`:

· **Atlas** — a sprite sheet sliced into a grid. This is the normal case. Drag the PNG in and Godot offers to auto-slice it; accept, and every non-empty cell becomes a tile.
· **Scene Collection** — each "tile" is an instanced scene. For doors, chests, torches — anything that needs a script. Expensive; use sparingly.

With an Atlas source selected, the **Setup** sub-tab controls the slicing (Texture Region Size, Separation, Margins). The **Select** sub-tab lets you click an individual tile and set its per-tile properties in the right panel.

Two per-tile things worth knowing now: **Texture Origin** moves a tile's art off its cell, which is how a tall tree occupies one cell but draws upward; and **Alternative Tiles** (the `+` on a selected tile) create rotated or flipped variants you can paint directly.

Then the **TileMap** tab to paint. Tools along the top:
· **Paint** (`D`), **Line** (`L`), **Rect** (`R`), **Bucket** (`B`), **Picker** (`P`), **Eraser** (`E`, or hold `Shift` while painting).
· Right-drag erases.
· Hold `Ctrl` with the bucket to fill only contiguous same-tile cells.

Select several tiles in the palette at once and the brush paints the pattern. That is how you lay a 3×3 building in one drag.
Terrain sets and autotiling:
Autotiling: paint a blob and the engine picks the right edge and corner tiles. In Godot 4 this is **terrains**, and the setup is fiddly once and then free forever.

1. TileSet Inspector > **Terrain Sets** > add one. Set its **Mode**: `Match Corners and Sides` (47 tiles, best looking), `Match Corners` (15), or `Match Sides` (15). Pick the one your art actually has tiles for.
2. Add a **terrain** inside the set and name it (`grass`, `stone`), and give it a colour.
3. TileSet tab > **Paint** sub-tab > Property = **Terrains** > select your terrain > paint which terrain each tile *belongs to*, and in Corners-and-Sides mode paint each tile's individual **peering bits** — the little triangles and squares around the tile's edge that say "this side connects to grass".

That third step is the laborious part. Do one terrain fully before starting a second.

Then in the TileMap tab, choose the terrain from the palette instead of a tile and paint — edges resolve themselves.

From code:

```gdscript
layer.set_cells_terrain_connect(cells, 0, 0)   # cells, terrain_set, terrain
layer.set_cells_terrain_path(cells, 0, 0)
```

`set_cells_terrain_connect` takes an array of `Vector2i` and fixes up all the neighbours too. That is the function for runtime-generated terrain.
Physics, navigation and occlusion layers:
Collision is defined **once per tile**, in the TileSet, and every painted instance gets it. No `CollisionShape2D` nodes, no bodies.

1. TileSet Inspector > **Physics Layers** > add one. Set its collision **Layer** and **Mask** bits here — the whole TileMapLayer answers on those bits.
2. TileSet tab > **Paint** sub-tab > Property = **Physics Layer 0** > select a tile > a polygon editor appears in the tile preview. The default button gives you a full-cell rectangle; or draw the polygon by hand for a slope.

Do the same for:
· **Navigation Layers** — a navigation polygon per tile, so the tilemap feeds pathfinding directly. This is far simpler than a separate `NavigationRegion2D` for tile-based maps.
· **Occlusion Layers** — a light-occluder polygon per tile, so 2D lights cast shadows off walls automatically.

A tile with no polygon on a layer simply does not participate, which is how floors and walls share one TileSet.

The TileMapLayer node then has `collision_enabled`, `navigation_enabled`, and `collision_visibility_mode` — set that last one to **Force Show** while building and you can see every shape in the running game.

Physics on a tilemap is cheap because the engine merges adjacent shapes. A hand-built wall of 400 StaticBody2D nodes is not the same thing at all.
NavigationRegion2D and baking a polygon:
Pathfinding needs to know where the walkable floor is. A `NavigationRegion2D` holds that as a polygon.

Add the node, then in the Inspector create a **New NavigationPolygon** on `navigation_polygon`. Two ways to fill it:

· **By hand** — the viewport toolbar gives you a polygon tool. Click to place points around the walkable area. Draw a second polygon *inside* it and it becomes a hole.
· **Baked** — set the `NavigationPolygon`'s **Source Geometry Mode** (Root Node Children / Group With Children / Group Explicit) and its **parsed geometry type** and **collision mask**, then click **Bake NavigationPolygon** in the toolbar. The engine walks the scene and builds the polygon from your actual collision shapes.

Baking is the one to use: the navmesh then follows the level geometry instead of being a second thing to keep in sync. Re-bake after moving walls. `region.bake_navigation_polygon()` does it from code, including at runtime for a generated level.

Agent Radius on the `NavigationPolygon` shrinks the walkable area inward by that many pixels, so agents do not clip corners. Set it to roughly your character's collision radius.

For a tile-based level you usually do not need this node at all — use the TileSet's Navigation Layers from the previous lesson, which generate the mesh from the painted tiles.

**Debug > Visible Navigation** draws the mesh in the running game. Use it; a navmesh you cannot see is a navmesh you cannot debug.
Avoidance, and collision layers and mask:
**Avoidance** stops agents walking through each other. Turn on `avoidance_enabled`, then route your velocity *through* the agent instead of applying it directly:

```gdscript
func _physics_process(_delta: float) -> void:
    var next := agent.get_next_path_position()
    agent.velocity = global_position.direction_to(next) * speed

func _on_velocity_computed(safe: Vector2) -> void:
    velocity = safe
    move_and_slide()
```

Connect `velocity_computed` to that handler. You set `agent.velocity` as a *request*; the server adjusts it against the neighbours and hands back a safe velocity. Setting `velocity` directly with avoidance on does nothing useful. `neighbor_distance`, `max_neighbors`, `time_horizon_agents` and `avoidance_priority` tune it.

**Layers and masks**, which govern all 2D physics and are worth stating exactly once:

· `collision_layer` — the bits this body **occupies**. "What I am."
· `collision_mask` — the bits this body **scans**. "What I look for."
· A detects B **iff** `A.collision_mask & B.collision_layer != 0`.

It is not symmetric. A player hurtbox on layer 2 scanning nothing, and an enemy hitbox on layer 3 scanning layer 2, means the hitbox finds the hurtbox and not the reverse — which is correct and deliberate.

**Name the layers**: Project Settings > Layer Names > 2D Physics. The Inspector then shows `Player`, `Enemy`, `World` instead of twenty unlabelled squares, and the bug where everything is on layer 1 because nobody could tell them apart goes away.
Control nodes, anchors and offsets:
`Control` is to UI what `Node2D` is to the world, and it does **not** use `position` and `scale` the way Node2D does. It uses anchors and offsets, and fighting that is the usual beginner experience.

· **Anchors** (`anchor_left/top/right/bottom`, 0..1) are fractions of the parent's rect. Anchor right at 1.0 and the node's right edge follows the parent's right edge.
· **Offsets** are pixels from the anchor.
· So an anchor of 0 with offset 20 is "20 px from the left"; an anchor of 1 with offset -20 is "20 px from the right"; and both anchors at 0 and 1 with offsets 20 and -20 is "20 px margin on both sides, stretching".

Do not set these by hand. Select the Control and use the **Layout** button in the viewport toolbar: Full Rect, Center, Top Wide, Bottom Right, and so on. `Ctrl+Shift+A`... no — the toolbar is the way. Anchors Preset does the arithmetic for you.

`size` and `position` exist but are the *result*. `custom_minimum_size` is what you set when a node needs to be at least a certain size.

Other essentials: `mouse_filter` — **Stop** (default, eats the click), **Pass** (handles it and lets it through), **Ignore** (invisible to the mouse). A full-screen Control with the default Stop is the reason your game stopped receiving clicks. `focus_mode` and `focus_neighbor_*` for keyboard and gamepad navigation.
Containers: VBox, HBox, Grid, Margin:
A `Container` **takes over the position and size of its children**. The anchors and offsets from the last lesson stop applying — the container decides, and the Inspector greys those fields out. This is a feature; learn to want it.

· **VBoxContainer** / **HBoxContainer** — a column or a row. `separation` in the theme overrides.
· **GridContainer** — `columns`, filled left to right. Inventories.
· **MarginContainer** — one child, with padding. The standard outermost node of any screen.
· **PanelContainer** — draws a background behind its child and sizes to it.
· **CenterContainer** — centres its child at its minimum size.
· **ScrollContainer** — scrolls an oversized child. The child needs its horizontal or vertical size flag set to Fill for this to behave.
· **HSplitContainer** / **VSplitContainer** — a draggable divider.
· **TabContainer** — one tab per child, named by the child.
· **AspectRatioContainer** — keeps a child's proportions.

The control you use *inside* a container is **Size Flags** (Inspector > Layout > Container Sizing): `Fill`, `Expand`, `Shrink Center`. **Expand** is the one that matters — children with Expand share the leftover space, in proportion to their `size_flags_stretch_ratio`. Two labels in an HBox, one with Expand, is how you push something to the right.

The habit: nest containers rather than positioning anything. `MarginContainer > VBoxContainer > [PanelContainer, HBoxContainer]` resizes correctly at every window size for free, and hand-placed UI does not.
Labels, buttons, and the nodes you will:
· **Label** — static text. `text`, `horizontal_alignment`, `autowrap_mode`, and `clip_text`. For a number that updates every frame this is the node.
· **RichTextLabel** — BBCode. Turn `bbcode_enabled` on and you get `[b]`, `[color=red]`, `[wave]`, `[shake]`, `[img]`, and custom effects. Dialogue, tooltips, item descriptions. `append_text()` adds without reparsing everything.
· **Button** — `pressed` signal, `text`, `icon`, `disabled`, `toggle_mode`, `button_group`. `BaseButton.button_group` with a `ButtonGroup` resource gives you radio behaviour.
· **TextureButton** — a button that is four textures (normal, pressed, hover, disabled) and no theme. Right for stylised UI.
· **Panel** / **NinePatchRect** — backgrounds. `NinePatchRect` stretches the middle and preserves the corners, which is how a dialogue box scales.
· **TextureRect** — an image, with `stretch_mode` and `expand_mode`.
· **ProgressBar** / **TextureProgressBar** — health bars. The texture version does radial fills.
· **LineEdit** / **TextEdit** — one line, many lines. `text_submitted` on Enter.
· **OptionButton**, **CheckBox**, **CheckButton**, **HSlider**, **SpinBox** — settings menus.
· **ItemList**, **Tree** — lists and hierarchies with selection.

Theme overrides live at the bottom of every Control's Inspector — per-node font, font size, colour and `StyleBox`. Fine for one-offs; for anything repeated, use a Theme.
Theme resources, and styling once instea:
A `Theme` is a resource mapping **control type > property name > value**. Set it on one Control and it applies to that node and all its descendants, which means setting it on the root of your UI styles the whole game.

Make one: FileSystem > New Resource > Theme > save as `res://ui/theme.tres`. Double-click it and the bottom panel becomes the theme editor.

Four kinds of item per type:
· **Colors** — `font_color`, `font_hover_color`.
· **Constants** — `separation`, `margin_left`, `outline_size`.
· **Fonts** and **Font Sizes**.
· **Styles** — a `StyleBox` per state (`normal`, `hover`, `pressed`, `disabled`, `focus`).

`StyleBoxFlat` is the one to learn: `bg_color`, `border_width_*`, `border_color`, `corner_radius_*`, `expand_margin_*`, and `anti_aliasing` — which you turn **off** for pixel art. `StyleBoxTexture` uses a nine-patch instead.

**Type variations** are the feature worth knowing: in the theme editor, add a type like `DangerButton` with `Base Type = Button`, style it, then set a button's `theme_type_variation = "DangerButton"`. One theme, several button looks, no per-node overrides.

Set the theme project-wide at Project Settings > GUI > Theme > Custom, and every Control in every scene picks it up. Then the default font and default font size there apply to the editor-less case too.

The discipline: a per-node override is a decision you will have to find again later. A theme item is a decision in one place.
CanvasLayer, and UI that ignores the cam:
UI parented into the world moves with the camera, which is wrong. `CanvasLayer` is the fix: its children are drawn in **their own 2D space**, unaffected by any `Camera2D`.

```
World (Node2D)
├── TileMapLayer
├── Player
└── HUD (CanvasLayer)
    └── MarginContainer
        └── ...
```

The HUD now sits at screen coordinates and stays put.

· `layer` — an integer deciding draw order between CanvasLayers. Higher draws on top. The default world is layer 0, so a HUD on 1 and a pause menu on 10 is the usual arrangement.
· `follow_viewport_enabled` + `follow_viewport_scale` — opt back **in** to the camera, with a scale factor. This is how you do parallax by hand: a background CanvasLayer following at 0.5.
· `visible` — hides the whole layer in one property, which is the cheapest pause menu toggle there is.
· `transform` — offset or shake the entire layer. Shaking the HUD layer rather than each element is one line.

`z_index` orders siblings *within* a layer; `layer` orders the layers. Mixing them up is the usual "why is my UI behind the player" — if the UI is not on a CanvasLayer, no `z_index` will reliably save it once the camera moves.

`ParallaxBackground` and `Parallax2D` exist for scrolling backdrops specifically; `Parallax2D` is the newer one and works without a dedicated root.
Camera2D: limits, smoothing, and zoom:
Add a `Camera2D` as a child of the player and it just works — `enabled` is on by default and the nearest enabled camera in the tree wins.

The properties that do the work:

· `zoom` — a `Vector2`, and it **multiplies**: `Vector2(2, 2)` means zoomed *in* twice, showing half as much. Non-integer zoom on pixel art produces uneven pixels; keep it at whole numbers.
· `position_smoothing_enabled` + `position_smoothing_speed` — the camera lags the target. Speed around 5 is a gentle follow; 20 is nearly rigid. This single setting is most of what "the camera feels good" means.
* `rotation_smoothing_enabled` + `rotation_smoothing_speed`.
· `limit_left` / `right` / `top` / `bottom` — the camera will not show past these world coordinates. Set them to the level bounds and the view never shows the void. `limit_smoothed` eases into them.
· `drag_horizontal_enabled` + `drag_*_margin` — a dead zone, so small movements do not move the camera.
· `offset` — shift the view. Tween this for screen shake, or shake the `CanvasLayer` transform instead.
· `ignore_rotation` — on by default; turn it off for a camera that rolls with the car.

Methods: `make_current()`, `reset_smoothing()` (after a teleport, or the camera glides across the level), `align()`, `get_screen_center_position()`.

For a camera that follows two players, or leads the direction of travel, give the camera its own node at the scene root and move it in `_process` toward a computed target. A camera parented to the player can only ever do one thing.
Viewport scaling, and the stretch mode f:
Project Settings > **Display > Window**:

· **Size > Viewport Width / Height** — the resolution your game is *designed* at. For pixel art, a small number: 320×180, 426×240, 640×360. All three scale to 1920×1080 by whole numbers.
· **Size > Window Width / Height Override** — the window the player actually gets. Set this to 1280×720 and develop at a sensible window size while the game thinks it is 320×180.
· **Stretch > Mode**:
  - `disabled` — no scaling, UI in real pixels.
  - `canvas_items` — the viewport is scaled; **2D positions stay in design coordinates but drawing happens at the real resolution**, so text and rotated sprites are crisp. The usual choice for high-resolution art.
  - `viewport` — the game renders into a small buffer and that buffer is scaled up. Every pixel is a true, chunky pixel. **This is the pixel-art choice.**
· **Stretch > Aspect**: `keep` (letterbox, never distorts — the safe default), `keep_width`, `keep_height`, `expand`, `ignore`.
· **Stretch > Scale Mode**: `fractional` or **`integer`**. For pixel art set `integer` — it only ever scales by whole numbers and black-bars the remainder, which is the difference between clean pixels and a shimmering mess.

Decide this at the start of a project. Changing the design resolution later moves every hand-placed coordinate in the game.

`get_window().content_scale_factor` and `DisplayServer.window_set_mode()` let you change it at runtime for a settings menu.
SubViewport, and rendering a scene into:
